findings.claim: Nelson Mandela, a Christian, spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid through protest rather than terrorism.
findings.truth: Mandela co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the ANC, in 1961 and led a sabotage campaign; the Rivonia Trial convicted him of sabotage and conspiracy against the state. The 27 years are right, but he is the wrong example for a paragraph arguing that faith inspires peace rather than violence, and the sentence tells a student the opposite of the truth about him. Desmond Tutu opposed apartheid without violence and is already used in lesson 3.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Nelson Mandela - 'co-founded the militant Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961 and led a sabotage campaign'; convicted of sabotage and conspiracy; served 27 years

findings.claim: Question 2 'Give two religious teachings about peace.' typed '1 mark - Give/Name', scheme '1 marks for each correct teaching, up to 2 marks ... [2 marks]'
findings.truth: Each theme is examined by one five-part question worth 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks, marked out of 24. There is no 2-mark part, and both short parts are single-point recall. Lesson 3 question 2 already uses the correct one-point form.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 - 'marks will be allocated as follows; 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12'; 'Each five-part question is worth 24 marks'

findings.claim: Question 3 sets the 4-mark question on forgiveness: 'Explain two similar religious beliefs in contemporary British society about forgiveness.'
findings.truth: The three issues on which this theme requires contrasting beliefs are violence, weapons of mass destruction and pacifism. Forgiveness is one of the three issues for the crime and punishment theme, so the 4-mark part of a peace and conflict question is not set on it. Lessons 2 and 3 set this question correctly (pacifism, weapons of mass destruction). Options: (a) leave it - forgiveness is taught inside this theme, so the practice is off-target rather than false; (b) re-set the question on violence, which this lesson teaches, and rewrite the scheme around the Quaker position and the self-defence position. Recommend (b).
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.4 (violence, weapons of mass destruction, pacifism) against spec 3.2.1.5 (corporal punishment, death penalty, forgiveness)
findings.ruling: Leave: 4-mark issue re-set belongs to the relabel queue.

findings.claim: 'The fuller seven-criteria version used today comes from the 1992 Catholic Catechism (CCC 2309), which added last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportional force, and civilian protection.' The same claim sits in the just war theory data-def ('CCC 2309, seven criteria').
findings.truth: Paragraph 2309 gives four conditions: the damage inflicted by the aggressor must be lasting, grave and certain; all other means must have been shown to be impractical or ineffective; there must be serious prospects of success; and the use of arms must not produce evils graver than the evil to be eliminated. It gives no seven-point list and says nothing about civilian protection, which the Catechism treats separately at 2312-2314. The seven criteria in the key fact are the standard summary of the tradition, not a Catechism text.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Just war theory - the four conditions of Catechism of the Catholic Church 2309 quoted in full; four criteria, no mention of civilians

findings.claim: many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace”
findings.truth: Islam means submission or surrender to God. It shares the Arabic root s-l-m with salaam, peace, which is why the two are linked, but the word itself does not mean peace. The 12-mark scheme in the same lesson uses the safer wording 'One meaning of Islam is peace' and is left alone.
findings.evidence: settled Arabic etymology: islam = submission, from the root s-l-m shared with salaam

findings.claim: Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,”
findings.truth: The line is best known as John Paul II's, from his address to the diplomatic corps on 13 January 2003 ('war is not always inevitable, it is always a defeat for humanity'). Francis has used the same words, usually crediting John Paul II. I could not confirm an independent Francis original from the sources open to me this session (biblegateway, quran.com, Wikipedia), so I have not edited it. Options: (a) leave it - Francis has certainly condemned war in these terms; (b) re-attribute the quotation to John Paul II and add that Francis repeats it. Recommend (b), after someone checks a Vatican source; the fix is one clause.
findings.evidence: not verifiable from the permitted sources; Wikipedia's Pope John Paul II article does not carry the 2003 address
findings.ruling: Re-attributed to John Paul II; Francis noted as repeating it.

findings.claim: Question 2 'Name two criteria of the just war theory.' typed '1 mark - Give/Name', scheme '1 marks for each correct criterion, up to 2 marks ... [2 marks]'
findings.truth: Same error as F2: the short parts of the five-part question are worth 1 mark each and ask for one point.

findings.claim: Other religious organisations involved in supporting victims of war include Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), and the Red Cross (founded on Christian principles of compassion).
findings.truth: The Red Cross is not a religious organisation. Henry Dunant's own faith moved him to found it, but the Movement is neutral and independent of any religion, the emblem is recorded as the Swiss flag with its colours reversed, and the Red Crescent and Red Crystal exist so that the symbol carries no faith. The spec asks for the work of one present day religious organisation, so a student who names the Red Cross names the wrong kind of body. Muslim Aid is an accurate British replacement.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Emblems of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement - emblem 'formed by reversing the colours of the flag of neutral Switzerland'; Red Crescent and Red Crystal adopted so the symbol is not religious

findings.claim: 'If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate' (Qur'an) - cited with no chapter or verse, in lesson 2 question 4 and again in lesson 3 content_html.
findings.truth: The quotation is Qur'an 16:126 (Abdel Haleem). The wording is accurate and the reference is simply missing, so this is a completeness point, not an error. Worth adding on the next content pass, because the 6-mark question credits a named source.
findings.evidence: quran.com 16:126 - 'If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered. But if you patiently endure, it is certainly best' (Khattab), same verse

findings.claim: Question type label '4 marks - Explain Similarities & Differences' in all three lessons, and lesson 1's exam tip naming 'the 4-mark “Explain similarities and differences” question'.
findings.truth: The paper sets either two similar or two contrasting beliefs, never both in one question, so the label names a question that does not exist. Lessons 2 and 3 label contrasting-belief questions with it. This is the corpus-wide question-type relabel queue, not a unit fix.
findings.evidence: question text in lessons 2 and 3 ('Explain two contrasting religious beliefs...') against their own type labels

summary: Scripture is sound throughout: Matthew 5:9, 5:39, 5:44, 6:14, 26:52, Luke 23:34, Micah 6:8, Mark 12:31, 2 Corinthians 5:18-19 and Qur'an 2:190, 2:256, 5:8, 5:32, 6:151, 22:39 and 42:40 are all quoted in a recognised translation with the right reference, and every knowledge-check key, match order and flashcard answer is correct. The real problems are Nelson Mandela taught as a believer who rejected armed struggle, the seven just war criteria attributed to Catechism 2309, 'Islam means peace', the Red Cross listed as a religious organisation, and two 1-mark practice questions that demand two answers for 2 marks.
